title: At a crossroads: How Beijing sees Manila’s South China Sea turn
gist: Written from a Beijing-informed vantage point, this piece argues that Manila's strategy of internationalising the South China Sea dispute has worked — pulling in US treaty assets, a returning Japan, and a widening circle of Western partners — and that Beijing's wager that a stabilising US–China relationship will strand the Philippines is likely a miscalculation. Marcos's reorientation is institutionalised via the Maritime Zones Act and 'archipelagic defence', both capitals are locked into incompatible narratives, and the authors warn that without an insulated crisis-management channel each new resupply clash becomes a test of national resolve.

insights.claim: Wang Yi's description of China–Philippines relations as standing at a crossroads was deliberate signalling — simultaneously a warning and an invitation to change course — delivered on the sidelines of the Manila ASEAN meetings on 22 July.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Treat 'crossroads' language from Beijing as a documented pre-escalation marker rather than diplomatic filler when reading Chinese statements on the Philippines.
insights.quote: correct, rational decisions about the path ahead
insights.locator: When China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Philippine counterpart

insights.claim: Beijing interpreted the 20 July Second Thomas Shoal clash on the eve of the ASEAN foreign ministers' meetings as deliberately timed by Manila to force the dispute onto a multilateral agenda.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Expect Chinese pre-positioning and heightened incident risk around future ASEAN and multilateral summit dates, since Beijing now assumes clashes are calendar-engineered.
insights.quote: Beijing did not read the timing as coincidence
insights.locator: So when Chinese and Philippine personnel came to blows

insights.claim: Beijing's rhetorical strategy attributes Philippine assertiveness to 'external forces' and unnamed military and law enforcement factions, casting China as the patient neighbour and Manila as a state led astray rather than as a sovereign actor with its own interests.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: This framing removes Beijing's ability to negotiate with Manila as a principal, structurally lowering the odds of a bilateral off-ramp.

insights.claim: Manila's publicising of nearly every coast-guard encounter and its rebuilding of the case on the 2016 arbitral award has lifted the Philippines from a bilateral irritant to one of the most vexing problems in China's periphery diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Publicity is the Philippine weapon system; the incident tempo is a function of Manila's information strategy, not just physical encounters at sea.
insights.quote: Marcos abandoned what it preferred as the quiet bilateralism of the Duterte years, publicised nearly every coast-guard encounter, and rebuilt his case on the 2016 arbitral award
insights.locator: For Beijing, this was never a quarrel over rocks and reefs alone

insights.claim: Manila has discovered that internationalising the dispute generates real leverage with Washington, Tokyo and other Western partners, so it may see little value in ever returning to quiet bilateralism.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: The base case is a persistently elevated, recurring incident tempo in the South China Sea rather than a return to managed quiet — a standing risk premium for regional shipping and defence exposure.
insights.quote: The Philippines has learned that internationalising its dispute with China pays – and that may not stop.
insights.locator: At a crossroads: How Beijing sees Manila’s South China Sea turn

insights.claim: A single Philippine maritime incident can now reach the agenda of a US–China summit, after Marcos secured a call in which Trump pledged to raise Manila's concerns with Xi Jinping.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Escalation transmission from a reef to superpower-summit level is now demonstrated — a small maritime event can move US–China risk sentiment directly.
insights.quote: a superpower’s prestige tethered to a reef
insights.locator: The more striking development is political

insights.claim: The 1951 US–Philippines Mutual Defence Treaty has moved from background guarantee to active instrument, backed by expanded American access under EDCA, retention of the Typhon system beyond its initial exercise deployment, and rotation of the NMESIS anti-ship system in 2025.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Persistent US land-based missile presence in the first island chain is now a fact on the ground, sustaining demand for anti-ship and long-range fires programmes across the region.
insights.quote: the Typhon system (Opens in new window) retained beyond its initial exercise deployment, and the NMESIS anti-ship system (Opens in new window) rotated in during 2025

insights.claim: Japan worries Beijing more than the United States does in the South China Sea, because the Reciprocal Access Agreement and the January 2026 military logistics accord give Tokyo a foothold in maritime Southeast Asia along the first island chain China is trying to break out of.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Japan-linked escalation risk in the South China Sea is systematically underweighted versus the US channel; watch Japanese logistics and access agreements as the sharper trigger.
insights.quote: a former occupying power re-entering the region along the first island chain China is trying to break out of – touches a more sensitive nerve
insights.locator: The second lever worries Beijing more: Japan

insights.claim: Chinese commentary has begun naming Japan rather than the United States as the power fuelling South China Sea tensions.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: A shift in Chinese rhetorical targeting toward Tokyo is an early indicator of where economic or maritime coercion is likely to land next.

insights.claim: A widening circle of Australia, Canada and European states has joined Philippine maritime cooperative activities and joint patrols, alongside US freedom-of-navigation operations that now draw ever-closer Chinese intercepts.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: More participants and tighter intercept distances raise the probability of an accidental collision involving a third-party navy, broadening who is exposed to a South China Sea incident.
insights.quote: Australia, Canada and European states have joined the Philippines in maritime cooperative activities and joint patrols, alongside continuing US freedom-of-navigation operations that draw ever-closer Chinese intercepts.
insights.locator: Behind this inner pair lies a widening circle

insights.claim: ASEAN was conspicuously absent from the July joint statement marking the tenth anniversary of the arbitral ruling, and Manila's own Southeast Asian neighbours have stayed near-silent, leaving its explicit diplomatic backing to partners outside the region.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: ASEAN will not function as a collective constraint on China; the bloc is a poor proxy for regional risk pricing on the South China Sea.
insights.quote: Conspicuously absent from it was ASEAN.
insights.locator: Conspicuously absent from it was ASEAN

themes.theme: Beijing's wager and why it may fail

insights.claim: Beijing's bet is that as the US and China stabilise their rivalry around an expected Xi–Trump summit, the space for the Philippines to exploit great-power friction shrinks and Washington will not compensate Manila for its losses.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: A US–China summit détente is exactly the scenario in which Beijing feels freest to press the Philippines — de-escalation at the top can mean escalation at the reef.
insights.quote: will never foot the bill for the Philippines’ losses
insights.locator: Its deeper wager is that Manila has misjudged the moment

insights.claim: Marcos's reorientation is institutionalised rather than personal — embedded in a Maritime Zones Act and armed forces retooled for archipelagic defence — so a successor would struggle to dismantle it quickly.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Philippine election risk is a weaker mean-reversion mechanism than markets assume; the pro-US posture and its procurement pipeline should persist past a change of president.
insights.quote: Marcos’s turn is no whim but an institutionalised reorientation

insights.claim: Beijing's hope that political turmoil in Manila reopens the door to Duterte-era accommodation may prove a costly miscalculation, since that more accommodating bilateral approach is unlikely to return.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: If Chinese policy is built on a wrong assumption about Philippine reversion, the correction — when it comes — is more likely to be coercive than conciliatory.
insights.quote: Beijing’s hope that turmoil in Manila reopens that door may prove a costly miscalculation

insights.claim: Both capitals are now invested in mutually exclusive public narratives — Beijing's of external subversion, Manila's of principled resistance — that leave little room for the quiet compromises which previously managed the dispute, and each clash hardens views further.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: Narrative lock-in makes de-escalation politically costly on both sides, implying a ratchet: incidents raise the floor of tension rather than mean-reverting.
insights.quote: Both capitals are now invested in narratives – Beijing’s of external subversion, Manila’s of principled resistance – that leave little room for the quiet compromises that once managed the dispute.
insights.locator: That is the hazard the metaphor obscures

insights.claim: Avoiding a slide into conflict requires a crisis-management channel insulated from public messaging and alliance politics, capable of handling resupply missions and incidents before either side turns them into tests of national resolve.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: The single highest-value de-escalation indicator to watch is the creation of a quiet bilateral resupply/incident hotline; its absence keeps tail risk elevated.
insights.quote: one able to handle resupply missions and incidents before either side turns them into tests of national resolve

insights.claim: China maintains that outside states are 'not a party' to the dispute while rejecting the 2016 arbitral award as illegal and void, leaving no legal or multilateral forum both sides accept.
insights.speaker: Xiaobo Liu
insights.so_what: With legal adjudication and multilateral mediation both foreclosed, the dispute can only be settled by physical presence — favouring continued militarisation on all sides.
insights.locator: For Beijing, this was never a quarrel over rocks and reefs alone
